messages.subject: Language assessment scoring
messages.body_plain:
Hi Dr. Chalmers,

I work for a company that develops and implements automated language proficiency assessments. To validate our tests, we have a subset of our pilot-test examinees take our test in conjunction with another well-established speaking proficiency test that we use to establish criterion and convergent validity. We use your mirt package for calibration and assembling tests. Based on these analyses, we build statistical models to predict what examinees would have scored on the external assessment based on their performance on our own assessment. We are at a stage where we would like to transition to implementing adaptive versions of our tests, and we would like to decouple the scoring of our assessments from that of the external assessments on which they are based. Thus, my question is this: What is the best way to go about doing this to ensure that a score of, say, 6 on our English test is equivalent to a score of 6 on our Spanish test?

Please let me know if this question requires more context or more than a brief response in this discussion group. We'd be delighted to set up a Zoom or Skype meeting to consult with you and compensate you for your time.

-Zac

messages.subject: Bifactor Latent Scores
messages.body_plain:
All,
I have a question about bifactor latent scores. I am conducting a bifactor model using GRM with the IPIP NEO-PI. The scale is 120 items where each superordinate factor (i.e. Agreeableness, Neuroticism, etc) is comprised of 24 items. I am conducting each bifactor separately and the model has the General factor as the superordinate trait and the grouping factors as the subordinate traits (i.e. for Neuroticism there is anger, hositility, anxiety etc). As expected the unidimensional GRM models do not fit (no bifactor) but show a normal latent trait distribution. However, with the bifactors the latent trait distributions are off. For example, extraversion spans from -5 to +20. Upon inspection the Extraversion mean theta is 0.07 and the SD is 1.71. The means are all close to 0 as one would expect in IRT. However, IRT is supposed to standardized the SD to 1 so that there is a normal distribution (ranging typically from -3 to +3). My question is two fold. First are bifactor models supposed to be standardized to a mean of 0 and an SD of 1? If so, is there some kind of conversion that needs to take place much as in the way the estimates have to be manually calculated for the Beta parameters by dividing the D parameter by alpha for the latent trait? Please note that the bifactor models all have adequate fit as represented by the RMSEA, CFI, and TLI. Any help in this matter would be greatly appreciated as I scrolled through the discussions on here and did not find anything about this topic. Thanks.
-Gene

On Wed, Oct 2, 2019 at 5:10 PM Gene a <mos...@gmail.com> wrote:
> All,
> I have a question about bifactor latent scores. I am conducting a bifactor model using GRM with the IPIP NEO-PI. The scale is 120 items where each superordinate factor (i.e. Agreeableness, Neuroticism, etc) is comprised of 24 items. I am conducting each bifactor separately and the model has the General factor as the superordinate trait and the grouping factors as the subordinate traits (i.e. for Neuroticism there is anger, hositility, anxiety etc). As expected the unidimensional GRM models do not fit (no bifactor) but show a normal latent trait distribution. However, with the bifactors the latent trait distributions are off. For example, extraversion spans from -5 to +20. Upon inspection the Extraversion mean theta is 0.07 and the SD is 1.71. The means are all close to 0 as one would expect in IRT. However, IRT is supposed to standardized the SD to 1 so that there is a normal distribution (ranging typically from -3 to +3).

That's not really true when you are studying secondary trait estimates. Variances of the latent traits depends on many factors, include the type of estimator you use (ML point estimates have much more variance, EAP and MAP estimates tend to have less due to shrinkage). Though +20 is a little on the high side, which might suggest lack of convergence for some patterns. You might want to inspect those vector patterns to see why the values were so extreme.

> My question is two fold. First are bifactor models supposed to be standardized to a mean of 0 and an SD of 1?

No. Though plausible value imputations will follow this form, but I don't think this is what you are after unless your goal is to perform some additional model-average inferences.

Phil

messages.subject_clean: Replicate multipleGroup() DIF detection result by DIF()
messages.body_plain:
Hi Phil, I have two questions about the DIF function. Thank you for writing such a helpful package!
My first question is when we were trying to run likelihood ratio DIF testing procedure, we first compute step by step by using the multipleGroup function in mirt. The code we used is:

itemname1 <- colnames(Resp1)
Sex1=as.character(Sex)
models <- 'F1 = 1-10'
refmod <- multipleGroup(Resp1, models, group = Sex1, SE=TRUE,invariance=c('free_means', 'free_var', itemname1))
# loop over items
estmodels1 <- vector('list', ncol(Resp1))
for(i in 1:ncol(Resp1))
  estmodels1[[i]] <- multipleGroup(Resp1, models, group = Sex1, verbose = FALSE, calcNull=FALSE,invariance=c('free_means', 'free_var', itemname1[-i]))
(anovas <- lapply(estmodels1, anova, object2=refmod, verbose=FALSE))
# family-wise error control
p <- do.call(rbind, lapply(anovas, function(x) x[2, 'p']))
p.adjust(p, method = 'BH')
which(p.adjust(p, method = 'BH')<0.05)  # flagged items are (4,5,6,9,10)

Then we tried to use the DIF function to replicate above result by running:

refmod <- multipleGroup(Resp1, models, group = Sex1, SE=TRUE,invariance=c('free_means', 'free_var', itemname1))
DIF(refmod, which.par = c('a1', 'd'), p.adjust = 'fdr',scheme = 'drop')  #the flagged DIF items are (4,5,6)

However, the result computed by DIF was different from the one by multipleGroup. We expected DIF, as a "wrapper to the multipleGroup function", to generate the same result as the multipleGroup function. May I ask why would this happen?

My second question is if we want to equate two groups by leaving "free_means" and "free_var" out of the invariance argument, what constraint would be set on the mean and variance of the two groups (like constrain the mean to be zero and variance to be one)?

Thank you in advance for your help!

-Ruoyi

Hi Jeannie,

Those interpretations are probably more suitable for the DRF statistics rather than the previously proposed area-based statistics in the 2016 paper. The sDTF shows scoring bias over the complete theta distribution, but the word 'average' is inaccurate here. If the theta distribution were uniform this interpretation would be correct, however, but in general the above quotation applies better to the signed DRF statistics. This is one reason why I generally recommend investigating those measures over the earlier variants. HTH.

Phil

messages.body_plain:
The 'weight' is more just an integral across a range of theta with equal weights for all values of θ. So, it still is an average, but it's not the kind of weighted average, weighted by g(θ), which is more what you want (hence, the DRF statistics). The description in the function is correct in that it still is an average, but more likely a weighted average is more meaningful. HTH.

Phil

It's very likely that some factor scores cannot be computed use the MAP estimator, or at least that no unique factor score was computable (hence the error about the hessian being non-invertible, which means the optimization surface is quite flat). If you can isolate the problematic cases then you may be able to use a stronger prior distribution, but overall there's not too much that can be done about cases like these without additional information.

Phil

messages.body_plain:
On Sun, Oct 27, 2019 at 2:40 PM Jeannie <jeann...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hi Phil,
>
> I'm using the DIF function in mirt to evaluate DIF and have a few questions:
>
> 1) when you identify you want an adjusted p-value in the DIF function and use a sequential DIF detection approach, are the items that are treated as non-invariant based on the adjusted p-value or the unadjusted pvalue? I think it is the adjusted p-value but want to confirm I'm understanding correctly.

Adjusted p-values.

>
> 2) i'm confused as to why the seq_stat details state that the drop sequential scheme identifies items as displaying DIF if using seq_stat = 0.05, for example, based on a p-value GREATER than 0.05 (versus based on a p-value LESS than 0.05)...? Using the drop_sequential approach in the DIF function, I have been identifying items as displaying DIF as those that have p < 0.05 in the final output...
>
> > "select a statistic to test for in the sequential schemes. Potential values are (in descending order of power) 'AIC', 'AICc', 'SABIC', 'HQ', and 'BIC'. If a numeric value is input that ranges between 0 and 1, the 'p' value will be tested (e.g., seq_stat = .05 will test for the difference of p < .05 in the add scheme, or p > .05 in the drop scheme), along with the specified p.adjust input. For models fitted with prior distributions 'DIC' is also supported, though for these models the p-value approach is not"

The add schemes will add the associated parameter equality constraints if (adjusted) p > .05, while drop schemes will remove the equality constraints if the more freely estimated model fits unusually better, p < .05. These are basically mirrors of each other. HTH.

Phil

No need, I just patched the issue. Turns out I didn't pass the required 'mins' internal to indicate what constitutes the lowest category in polytomous items (sometimes its 0, sometimes 1....but it could be anything). This created the incorrect dummy matrices internally, which is why the results were inconsistent with the ML estimator. The latest dev now provides .908..... for both inputs after using the corrected extract.group() function. Thanks for the report!

Phil
